nodes.label: Hot 100 Algorithm Practice
nodes.description: Connect seventeen categories and one hundred problems covering hashing, windows, trees and graphs, backtracking, binary search, heaps, greedy algorithms, and dynamic programming.
nodes.question: How do problem constraints determine states, invariants, and correctness?

nodes.label: 0/1 Knapsack / Unbounded Knapsack
nodes.description: In 0/1 knapsack each item may be used at most once; unbounded knapsack permits reuse. One-dimensional implementations need the corresponding traversal order.
explanation: Coin Change and Perfect Squares can use the amount or target value as the state and choose the final denomination or square. Target zero needs zero items; initialize other states as unreachable, then minimize the count using smaller states. Initializing every amount to zero makes unreachable states appear better than valid solutions.

A denomination can be reused, giving an unbounded-knapsack problem. In a one-dimensional implementation that loops over items, capacities are usually processed in increasing order. Minimizing the number of coins is different from counting combinations; for counting, loop order also determines whether different permutations are counted repeatedly.
nodes.boundary: With items in the outer loop, 0/1 capacities are usually traversed backward and unbounded capacities forward. Also distinguish counting from optimization.

nodes.label: Activation Checkpointing
nodes.description: Store fewer intermediate activations and recompute them during backpropagation, trading computation time for GPU memory.
explanation: Activation checkpointing avoids saving every intermediate activation and recomputes some during backpropagation, trading extra computation for GPU memory. A model checkpoint instead saves model or training state for recovery or deployment. Both use the word checkpoint, but solve different problems. Gradient accumulation, parameter sharding and freezing some parameters can also reduce GPU memory use, each with computational or capability tradeoffs.
nodes.boundary: This differs from saving a model checkpoint for recovery.

nodes.label: Adagrad / RMSProp
nodes.description: Adagrad accumulates squared gradients; RMSProp uses an exponential moving average of squared gradients to adapt per-parameter update scales.
explanation: AdaGrad scales each parameter’s update using its past gradients. This is useful for sparse features, but cumulative statistics can make effective step sizes increasingly small. RMSProp uses moving averages of recent squared gradients to limit that continual decay. These are adaptive step-size methods: parameters can receive different effective update scales. Adaptive does not mean that the learning rate needs no tuning or that validation is unnecessary.
nodes.boundary: Adaptation still requires setting and validating the learning rate.

nodes.label: Adam / AdamW
nodes.description: Adam uses first- and second-moment estimates of gradients to scale updates; AdamW applies weight decay separately from that adaptive scaling.
explanation: Adam combines a moving average of gradients with statistics of squared gradients, giving both momentum and per-parameter scaling. Its beta parameters control how long past information is retained. Epsilon is a small numerical stabilizer, not an exploration probability. Check the context when the same parameter name appears in different algorithms. Adam is convenient for many deep learning tasks but is not universally the best optimizer in theory or practice.
nodes.boundary: AdamW changes how weight decay is applied; it is not simply a faster version of Adam.

nodes.label: Agent
nodes.description: A system that organizes models, tools, feedback, and an execution loop around a goal and state.
explanation: A fixed workflow arranges major steps such as retrieval, generation and review in advance. An agent loop chooses the next tool or action from current results. ReAct alternates reasoning, action and observation. More autonomous decisions do not necessarily improve reliability. Repeated tasks often suit fixed processes, while open-ended tasks require more dynamic choices. Both can be combined without turning the whole system into an unconstrained loop.
nodes.boundary: Generating a tool call does not by itself create a reliable task-execution loop.

nodes.label: API — Application Programming Interface
nodes.description: The calling conventions that software exposes to other programs, including input, output, and error behavior.
nodes.boundary: Interface conventions and internal implementations should be understood separately.

nodes.label: Attention / Transformer
nodes.description: Attention aggregates information according to relevance; a Transformer organizes sequence computation using attention and related modules.
explanation: Intuitively, a query represents what the current position seeks, keys provide matching clues at other positions, and values contain the information to aggregate. Attention scores determine aggregation weights after normalization. This is an analogy: queries, keys and values are learned vectors, not human-written questions, catalogs and answers. A high attention weight does not automatically establish interpretable causal importance to the final output.
nodes.boundary: Attention weights do not automatically provide a causal explanation.

nodes.label: Backtracking / Pruning
nodes.description: Explore a choice tree, undo path state on return, and prune branches that cannot produce valid answers.
explanation: Backtracking expands choices into a search tree: choose, explore recursively, then undo the choice on return. Permutations use a used marker so each element is chosen once. Subsets use an increasing start index so different selection orders do not enumerate the same set repeatedly. Define the state first, then choose used markers, a starting index, or a remaining target.

Copying the current path is usually required when adding it to an answer. If you only save a reference to the same mutable list, undoing it later will change all answers together. Backtracking is not an antonym of dynamic programming; memoization is also possible when different search paths have the same subsequent state.
nodes.boundary: Pruning depends on the problem constraints, and enumeration cost is also bounded below by the output size.

nodes.label: Batch Size
nodes.description: The number of samples processed in one forward pass. Gradient accumulation and data parallelism can increase the effective batch size used for an update.
explanation: A batch is a collection of samples processed together, and batch size is its sample count. An iteration usually means one execution of the training loop, although the code’s definition matters. An optimizer step is an actual parameter update. An epoch usually means one complete pass through a finite training dataset.

With 1,000 training samples and batches of 100, dropping no samples and updating once per batch gives ten batches and ten parameter updates per epoch. This is one epoch with ten update steps, not ten epochs. With streaming corpora or very large datasets, researchers may report optimizer steps or tokens processed rather than complete passes through the data.
nodes.boundary: Distinguish between per-device micro-batches and global effective batches.

nodes.label: BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm
nodes.description: Normalize activations using different statistical scopes and formulas to change network computation and training behavior.
explanation: Batch normalization uses minibatch statistics to normalize intermediate activations, then applies learnable parameters to preserve expressive capacity. It is common in convolutional networks. Very small training batches or large differences between devices’ batches can make the statistics unstable. Inference usually uses running statistics accumulated during training, rather than statistics from the current individual sample. Incorrect training or evaluation modes can therefore change outputs unexpectedly.
nodes.boundary: During training, BatchNorm typically uses minibatch statistics. LayerNorm normalizes features within each sample; RMSNorm does not subtract the mean.

nodes.label: BCE — Binary Cross-Entropy
nodes.description: Score binary probability predictions, penalizing confident rejection of the true outcome more strongly.
explanation: BCE is commonly used for binary classification and for each label in multilabel learning. It compares predicted probabilities with target labels, rather than merely counting correct class decisions. Think of it as scoring probability predictions: the less probability assigned to the true answer, the greater the penalty.

Consider an email that is actually spam. Model A assigns a 49% probability of spam; model B assigns only 1%. With a 50% classification threshold, both are wrong, so accuracy cannot distinguish these errors. But model B almost rules out the true answer and is more confidently wrong, so BCE penalizes it more. Probability prediction quality and the final hard classification are different things.

In multilabel image recognition, the model can separately predict whether an image contains a cat, a dog or a car, then combine the BCE losses for those labels. Separate loss terms do not imply that the labels are independent in the real world; a shared network can still use their correlations. If exactly one of cat, dog or bird must be chosen, model the classes as mutually exclusive instead.
nodes.boundary: Used for binary classification and per-label multilabel tasks; it measures more than thresholded correctness.

nodes.label: BCEWithLogitsLoss
nodes.description: Accept logits directly and combine sigmoid with BCE in a numerically stable computation.
explanation: BCELoss expects probabilities as input. BCEWithLogitsLoss accepts raw logits and combines sigmoid with BCE internally. This fused computation improves numerical stability by avoiding problems caused by first forming extreme probabilities. Do not apply sigmoid separately before BCEWithLogitsLoss. You need not memorize the API for an interview, but should understand that WithLogits means scores before the probability transformation.
nodes.boundary: Targets should be floating-point tensors with matching shape. Do not apply sigmoid to the input again.

nodes.label: BFS / DFS
nodes.description: BFS explores vertices layer by layer; DFS explores one branch before backtracking.
explanation: Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore nodes one step away before those two steps away. When every edge has the same cost, it therefore finds a path with the fewest steps. Depth-first search uses recursion or an explicit stack to follow a path deeply and backtrack when needed. It suits dependency analysis, connectivity structure, and backtracking. Finding a path with DFS does not mean finding a shortest path. Both searches must track visited states to avoid looping indefinitely around cycles.
nodes.boundary: BFS finds paths with the fewest edges. These need not have minimum total cost when edge weights differ.

nodes.label: Binary / Multiclass / Multilabel
nodes.description: Distinguish two possible outcomes, one choice among mutually exclusive classes, and multiple labels that may hold simultaneously.
explanation: Binary classification answers a yes/no question, such as whether an email is spam. Multiclass single-label classification chooses one of several mutually exclusive answers, such as cat, dog, or bird as the main species. Multilabel classification allows several answers simultaneously, such as both cats and dogs in an image. It usually assigns each label a separate probability without requiring them to sum to one. This distinction directly affects the output layer and loss; class count alone cannot determine whether BCE or mutually exclusive categorical cross-entropy is appropriate.
nodes.boundary: Determine the task semantics before selecting outputs and loss.

nodes.label: BM25 / HNSW
nodes.description: BM25 scores documents using term-matching statistics; HNSW accelerates approximate nearest-neighbor search using a hierarchical graph.
explanation: An inverted index maps a term to documents containing it, avoiding a full document scan. TF-IDF considers both a term’s prominence within a document and its rarity across the collection. BM25 adds term-frequency saturation and document-length adjustments. Rare product identifiers and exact terminology often suit keyword retrieval; paraphrases with different wording may need semantic representations. BM25 is not a generative language model.
nodes.boundary: An index cannot compensate for an unsuitable vector representation.

nodes.label: Boosting
nodes.description: Add models in successive rounds to improve their combination; methods differ in objectives and weighting rules.
explanation: Gradient boosting adds models sequentially to improve the current ensemble. With squared error, a new tree can be understood as predicting unexplained residuals; with other losses, fitting negative loss gradients is more accurate. GBDT uses decision trees as gradient-boosting base learners. Each round adds a correction rather than training a wholly independent complete model.

The learning rate controls each new tree's contribution; tree count controls the number of rounds. Smaller contributions often require more rounds to reach a given training error, so consider both together. Maximum depth and leaf count constrain each correction's complexity. Training corrections do not guarantee improvement on validation every round, so early stopping is common.
nodes.boundary: Boosting methods cannot all be described as fitting the same type of residual.

nodes.label: Bootstrap / OOB
nodes.description: Sample with replacement to form training data. A tree can evaluate examples not selected in its bootstrap sample.
explanation: Bootstrap sampling draws training examples with replacement, so some repeat and others are omitted. Bagging trains models on different resamples and combines their predictions, hoping their incidental errors partly cancel. Copying the same model repeatedly does not help: if all models make identical errors, averaging cannot fix them. Diversity and individual model quality both matter.
nodes.boundary: Out-of-bag evaluation does not replace appropriate temporal or group-based validation.

nodes.label: Broadcasting
nodes.description: Use shape rules to extend the meaning of operations on smaller tensors without explicit copying.
explanation: Dtype is the numeric representation, such as integer or floating point. Device specifies where data and computation reside, such as CPU or GPU. Broadcasting lets smaller-shaped data participate in operations with larger-shaped data under defined rules, without manually copying it—for example, adding the same bias to each feature across a batch. Broadcasting can also make an incorrectly shaped computation run, so absence of an error does not prove correctness. Padding fills positions in unequal-length sequences; a mask tells computation which positions are valid.
nodes.boundary: A valid broadcast can still compute the wrong quantity.

nodes.label: Calibration
nodes.description: Check whether the reported probabilities match the actual long-term occurrence rates.
explanation: Calibration asks whether reported probabilities are trustworthy: among events assigned an 80% probability, do about 80% occur over the long run? A model can rank well yet produce overconfident probabilities, giving high AUC but poor calibration. The Brier score measures the difference between probabilities and binary outcomes. Temperature scaling adjusts output score magnitudes while preserving some ranking structure, and is often used for post-hoc calibration. Fit it on appropriately held-out data. Do not use test labels to improve the model and then report the same test as an independent evaluation.
nodes.boundary: A high AUC does not guarantee well-calibrated probabilities.

nodes.label: Canonical Key
nodes.description: Eliminate unimportant representation differences and generate identical index keys for the same equivalence class.
explanation: The difficulty with anagram grouping is not how to append the list, but constructing the same keys for the same class of objects. The sorted character sequence can be used as the key; when the question is limited to lowercase English letters, the twenty-six character count can also be used as the key. For example, the character order of eat and tea is different, but the frequency array is the same. This idea is called normalized representation: eliminating unimportant order differences.

Keys must be unambiguous. Do not concatenate multiple counts into a number string without separation, otherwise different counts may result in the same string. Sorting keys incur additional character sorting costs; counting keys for a fixed alphabet can be constructed linearly based on the total number of characters, but the twenty-six position premise cannot be directly generalized to all character sets.
nodes.boundary: Character counts can identify anagrams. Composite keys must encode those counts unambiguously.

nodes.label: Checkpoint / Resume / Seed
nodes.description: Save training state to resume later; seeds help control random processes.
explanation: A checkpoint saves training state. Model weights alone are usually sufficient for inference. Resuming training faithfully may also require optimizer state, scheduler progress, random-number-generator state and the data-loading position. A random seed helps control initialization and data shuffling, but hardware differences and nondeterministic operations can still change results. Reproducibility concerns the whole process, not just recording a seed.
nodes.boundary: Weights alone usually do not support exact continuation, and seeds do not guarantee identical results across environments.

nodes.label: Concurrency / Parallelism
nodes.description: Concurrency allows tasks to make progress over overlapping periods; parallelism executes tasks simultaneously.
nodes.boundary: Asynchrony describes waiting and control flow and is not equivalent to parallelism.

nodes.label: Contrastive Loss
nodes.description: Learn useful representations from positive and negative relationships or other contrastive structures.
explanation: Metric learning studies similarity in a representation space. Contrastive loss brings related representations closer while separating unrelated ones. Triplet loss uses an anchor, a positive sample and a negative sample, aiming to place the positive closer to the anchor than the negative. InfoNCE often frames learning as finding the correct match among a batch of candidates. These ideas support image–text alignment, semantic retrieval and face verification. Negative samples may actually be related to the anchor; such false negatives create misleading training pressure.
nodes.boundary: The definition of positive and negative pairs is itself a key assumption.

nodes.label: CPU / GPU
nodes.description: CPUs handle complex control flow and varied operations; GPUs excel at large workloads with many similar operations that can run in parallel.
explanation: Scenario and inputs: A program takes 100 seconds. A GPU can accelerate 80 seconds of work by 10×; the other 20 seconds remain unchanged. Initially ignore transfer overhead.
Step 1: The accelerated portion falls from 80 seconds to 8, giving 28 seconds in total.
Step 2: Overall speedup is 100/28≈3.57, not 10.
Step 3: Even eliminating all 80 seconds leaves 20 seconds, limiting speedup to 5×. Real transfers and scheduling also affect the result.
Result and explanation: Amdahl’s law shows why an individual kernel’s speedup must be assessed in the context of end-to-end runtime.
Pitfalls and limits: The analysis assumes fixed workload and accelerated fraction. Larger batches or another algorithm can change that fraction and require fresh measurement.
Try another condition: If only 10% of time can be accelerated, what is the limit even at infinite speed?
Self-check answer: 1/0.9≈1.11×.
nodes.boundary: GPUs are not faster for every task.

nodes.label: Cross-Entropy / NLL
nodes.description: Classification cross-entropy relates to the negative log probability of the true class; NLL applies to more general likelihood models.
explanation: Cross-entropy is not an alternative to BCE: BCE is cross-entropy for the binary case. In training code, CrossEntropyLoss commonly accepts raw scores for multiple classes and performs the appropriate normalization internally. A typical task has one correct class per sample. Next-token prediction uses the same kind of classification objective over the vocabulary. Negative log-likelihood, or NLL, penalizes a model for assigning low likelihood to observed data. Cross-entropy for discrete classification is closely related to NLL, but likelihood-based objectives are not limited to classification.
nodes.boundary: PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss expects raw scores, while NLLLoss expects log probabilities.

nodes.label: Cross-Validation
nodes.description: Evaluate a training procedure across several data splits, using nested validation when model selection must be isolated.
explanation: Cross-validation evaluates stability across repeated data splits. Out-of-fold predictions, or OOF predictions, come from a fold model that did not see the corresponding sample during training; stacking commonly uses them. Nested cross-validation performs model selection in an inner loop and evaluates the whole selection procedure in an outer loop, reducing optimism from repeated tuning. It costs more computation and does not eliminate distribution shift. The time-based or group-based splitting rules must still be appropriate.
nodes.boundary: Time-dependent or grouped data cannot be split randomly without considering its structure.

nodes.label: CTC — Connectionist Temporal Classification
nodes.description: Sum the probabilities of valid alignment paths when sequence labels are not aligned to individual input time steps.
explanation: CTC, connectionist temporal classification, handles tasks where input frames and output labels lack a known alignment. In speech recognition, for example, the transcript may be known without knowing which frames correspond to each sound. CTC sums over possible alignments using a collapse rule that merges consecutive repeated labels before removing a dedicated blank symbol. Label smoothing softens the target distribution to discourage overconfidence. Auxiliary losses add training signals for intermediate representations, load balancing or other goals. Adding a loss does not automatically help; objectives and their weights can conflict.
nodes.boundary: CTC assumes monotonic alignments and compatible sequence lengths; it does not align arbitrary sequence pairs.

nodes.label: Data Leakage
nodes.description: Unintentionally use information unavailable at prediction time during training or model selection.
nodes.boundary: Preprocessing statistics and target encoding can also leak validation information.

nodes.label: Dice Loss
nodes.description: Define a training objective from the overlap between predicted and target regions, commonly for segmentation.
explanation: IoU, intersection over union, measures overlap between predicted and ground-truth regions. Dice is another common overlap measure and can be used to construct a training loss. In medical imaging, a model may miss a small lesion entirely yet achieve high pixel accuracy by correctly predicting the background. Region-overlap metrics make this failure easier to see. Segmentation often combines BCE or cross-entropy with Dice-based objectives to assess both individual pixels and overall overlap. Distinguish differentiable training approximations from the metrics used in formal evaluation.
nodes.boundary: Smoothing terms and reduction conventions differ across implementations and affect the result.

nodes.label: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
nodes.description: Repeatedly settle the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relax its outgoing edges.
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm maintains the best distances discovered so far, repeatedly selects the nearest unfinalized node, and uses it to improve its neighbors' distances. With nonnegative edge weights, this nearest node can be finalized safely: extending a path cannot suddenly make it cheaper through a negative edge. Navigation and nonnegative-cost networks are typical uses. A priority queue accelerates selecting the next node. Dijkstra is not a universal shortest-path algorithm for arbitrary weighted graphs.
nodes.boundary: The standard algorithm is not generally valid when edges may have negative weights.

nodes.label: DPO / GRPO
nodes.description: DPO typically uses preference pairs; GRPO constructs update signals from relative rewards within sampled groups of outputs.
explanation: DPO directly optimizes relative response preferences from preference data. Its classic form uses a reference model, without first fitting a separate reward network and then running online policy optimization. IPO, KTO and ORPO are other preference optimization approaches, differing in objectives, feedback formats or dependence on reference models. You need not memorize every objective here. These are methods for training existing models from preferences, rather than new Transformer architectures. Choose according to the available data.
nodes.boundary: Their feedback formats and sampling/training procedures differ.

nodes.label: Dreamer / MuZero
nodes.description: Dreamer trains policies on imagined trajectories in a learned latent dynamics model; MuZero combines a learned model with search.
explanation: Dreamer learns a latent world model from real interaction experience, then rolls out imagined trajectories inside that model to train an actor and a critic. It aims to turn each real experience into many internal learning opportunities, improving sample efficiency. The key distinction is training an action policy inside the model; this need not involve a large new search before every real action. Model prediction errors affect the policy, so real data must continually correct the model.
nodes.boundary: Compare control objectives, prediction targets, and planning mechanisms.

nodes.label: Dropout
nodes.description: Randomly mask some activations during training to reduce dependence on particular pathways.
explanation: Dropout randomly masks activations during training to reduce reliance on particular information pathways. Inference normally disables this masking, with scaling handled according to the implementation. Dropout does not permanently delete neurons after training. Drop path and stochastic depth randomly skip paths or residual branches in suitable architectures, providing more structured stochastic regularization. Their benefit depends on the architecture and data; adding more does not always help.
nodes.boundary: Standard inference does not permanently delete neurons.

nodes.label: Dtype / Device
nodes.description: Dtype specifies numerical representation; device specifies where data and operations reside, such as a CPU or GPU.
explanation: Dtype is the numeric representation, such as integer or floating point. Device specifies where data and computation reside, such as CPU or GPU. Broadcasting lets smaller-shaped data participate in operations with larger-shaped data under defined rules, without manually copying it—for example, adding the same bias to each feature across a batch. Broadcasting can also make an incorrectly shaped computation run, so absence of an error does not prove correctness. Padding fills positions in unequal-length sequences; a mask tells computation which positions are valid.
nodes.boundary: Matching shapes do not guarantee matching dtypes or devices.

nodes.label: Dummy Node
nodes.description: Place an auxiliary node before a linked list’s actual head so changes at the head and elsewhere can use the same pointer operations.
explanation: Linked list questions need to distinguish between node identity and node value. Two nodes with the same value do not mean that the linked lists intersect. The sentinel or dummy node is placed before the real head, so that operations such as deleting the head node and inserting the head can also be written as "modify the next of the predecessor". When deleting the nth node from the last, the fast and slow pointers maintain a fixed distance, so that the slow pointer finally falls on the predecessor of the node to be deleted. The bounds should be derived from loop invariants, not just by reciting how many times the fast pointer has been moved.
nodes.boundary: Return the actual head node; do not use sentinel values as input data.

nodes.label: Dynamic Programming
nodes.description: Save reusable subproblem results and solve them according to defined states and transitions.
explanation: The central question in dynamic programming is not how to fill a table, but how to define the state. A state should retain information needed for future decisions without carrying irrelevant history. In a knapsack problem, for example, the current item and remaining capacity define the state; given these, the order in which earlier items were considered usually no longer matters.

If different choice sequences reach the same state, its best result can be computed once and reused: this is an overlapping subproblem. Optimization also requires that the current optimum can be constructed from suitable subproblem optima, usually called optimal substructure. Top-down memoization solves and caches states when encountered; bottom-up computation evaluates them in dependency order.

Examples include knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, and certain path problems. The number of states can be enormous; adding several dimensions can cause state explosion. Dynamic programming does not make every combinatorial problem cheap. In an interview, explain that a suitable state definition merges subproblems that recur along different paths, using stored intermediate results to avoid repeated search.
nodes.boundary: Memoization alone is insufficient; state meanings and boundaries must also be clear.

nodes.label: Early Stopping / Patience
nodes.description: Stop according to validation performance; patience specifies how long improvement may be absent.
explanation: During training, periodically evaluate on validation data that was not used to fit the model. Falling training error alongside persistently worsening validation error is a common sign of overfitting. Early stopping ends training based on validation performance and usually retains a better checkpoint. Patience is the allowed number of consecutive checks without improvement, not necessarily seconds or epochs. Repeatedly using the test set to decide when to stop destroys its value as an independent evaluation.
nodes.boundary: Patience usually counts validation checks, so state its unit.

nodes.label: EM / Viterbi
nodes.description: EM iteratively estimates parameters in models with latent variables; Viterbi finds the most likely hidden-state sequence for a given model.
explanation: Latent variables are unobserved internal variables used to explain data—for example, a customer's unknown group given observed spending. EM alternates estimating hidden-variable probabilities under current parameters and updating parameters using those estimates. In a GMM, it repeatedly estimates component memberships and updates the components. Under suitable conditions the objective does not worsen, but a global optimum is not guaranteed.
nodes.boundary: Estimating model parameters differs from decoding a hidden-state sequence.

nodes.label: F1 Score
nodes.description: Combine precision and recall through their harmonic mean; a low value of either limits F1.
explanation: Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.
nodes.boundary: Specify averaging conventions such as macro or micro when comparing multiclass results.

nodes.label: Fast and Slow Pointers
nodes.description: Use different pointer speeds to find a midpoint or detect a cycle, then equal speeds to locate its entry.
explanation: A fast pointer taking two steps and a slow pointer taking one can find a midpoint or detect a cycle. Without a cycle, the fast pointer reaches null first; with a cycle, the pointers must meet inside it. To find the cycle entry, reset one pointer to the head, then advance both at the same speed. Their next meeting point is the entry. This follows from the relationship between the head-to-entry distance and distances around the cycle.

To test whether a linked list is a palindrome, find a midpoint, reverse the second half, and compare corresponding values using constant auxiliary space. Restore the second half if the caller expects the input unchanged. The pointer initialization determines which of the two middle nodes is selected for an even-length list.
nodes.boundary: The first meeting point is usually not the cycle entry, and null checks remain necessary.

nodes.label: Focal Loss
nodes.description: Reduce the relative contribution of easy samples so that training focuses more on difficult samples.
explanation: Focal loss reduces the relative loss contribution of easy, correctly classified samples so that training focuses more on difficult ones. This is useful in object detection, where easy background locations can greatly outnumber objects. Rather than assigning a fixed minority-class weight, it adjusts a sample’s contribution according to the model’s current prediction. Difficult samples may also be mislabeled, so focal loss is not a universal remedy for class imbalance. Assess it alongside label quality, sampling and evaluation metrics.
nodes.boundary: Difficult examples may be mislabeled. Emphasizing them does not guarantee better performance.

nodes.label: Forward / Backward
nodes.description: Compute predictions forward through a graph and loss gradients with respect to parameters backward through it.
explanation: The forward pass maps inputs to predictions. The loss function compares predictions with targets. Backpropagation computes how each parameter affects the loss: its gradient. The optimizer then updates parameters using those gradients and its own state. Backpropagation calculates gradients rather than updating parameters. Adam and SGD are update methods, rather than alternative network architectures. This sequence is fundamental to understanding training code.
nodes.boundary: Backpropagation does not itself update parameters.

nodes.label: Gradient
nodes.description: Describe the local rate of change along each parameter direction, guiding how updates affect loss.
explanation: The forward pass maps inputs to predictions. The loss function compares predictions with targets. Backpropagation computes how each parameter affects the loss: its gradient. The optimizer then updates parameters using those gradients and its own state. Backpropagation calculates gradients rather than updating parameters. Adam and SGD are update methods, rather than alternative network architectures. This sequence is fundamental to understanding training code.
nodes.boundary: Gradient direction and the eventual update size are different quantities.

nodes.label: Gradient Clipping
nodes.description: Limit a gradient norm or its components to reduce instability from unusually large gradients.
explanation: Gradient clipping limits the magnitude of gradients in an update. Norm-based clipping commonly rescales the whole gradient when its norm is too large, preserving its overall direction; value-based clipping bounds individual components. This differs from reducing the learning rate: clipping targets unusually large gradients, whereas the learning rate sets the overall scale of updates. Excessive clipping can slow learning. It cannot compensate for incorrect labels or a faulty loss implementation.
nodes.boundary: With gradient scaling, normally unscale before clipping.

nodes.label: Hash Table
nodes.description: Map keys to storage locations to support efficient key lookups.
nodes.boundary: Expected constant-time lookup is not an unconditional worst-case guarantee.

nodes.label: Huber Loss
nodes.description: Behave like squared error for small residuals and absolute error for large residuals.
explanation: Huber loss behaves like squared error for small errors and more like absolute error for large errors, balancing smoothness and robustness to outliers. Quantile loss, also called pinball loss, assigns different costs to overestimation and underestimation to learn a conditional quantile. Inventory planning, for example, may require a conservative high-demand quantile as well as average demand. Choose a loss based on what should be predicted and the costs of different errors, rather than the popularity of an abbreviation.

Interview answer: BCE is used for binary probability predictions and strongly penalizes confidently wrong predictions. Mutually exclusive multiclass tasks commonly use multiclass cross-entropy. For continuous-value prediction, consider MSE, MAE or Huber loss. Model architecture and loss function are separate choices; the same network can be trained with different objectives.
nodes.boundary: The transition scale still needs to suit the task.

nodes.label: In-place Marking
nodes.description: Use part of the input storage to record pending operations or visited state, reducing auxiliary space.
explanation: When setting zero in a matrix, you cannot immediately change the rows and columns as soon as you see zero, otherwise the newly created zeros will continue to propagate. First record which rows and columns need to be changed to zero, and then execute them uniformly. To compress the mark space, you can use the first row and first column as marks, but you should save whether the first row and first column originally contain zeros. Process the first row and column last to avoid overwriting the mark before it is used up.
nodes.boundary: This modifies the input. Preserve information in marker positions or process it in a safe order.

nodes.label: Index
nodes.description: Maintain additional lookup structures to reduce the data that queries need to scan.
explanation: An inverted index maps a word or feature back to documents containing it, supporting keyword search. A bitmap index represents records with a particular value as bits, turning multiple-condition filtering into fast bitwise operations for certain analytical workloads. These are not more advanced B+ trees; they target different query structures. A database may maintain several indexes and let its planner choose among them. Ask about query conditions before choosing an index.
nodes.boundary: Query benefits come with write and storage maintenance costs.

nodes.label: Initialization / Residual Connection
nodes.description: Initialization chooses starting parameter values; residual connections let a branch learn a change relative to its input.
explanation: Initialization determines the starting point of training. Using the same weights for all neurons may not break the symmetry; the scale may be too large or too small, making it difficult to propagate information and gradients. Xavier and He initialization are common methods for selecting initial scales based on layer structure and activation properties. They help get started with training and do not directly impart knowledge to the model. The weights of the pre-trained model have come from learning, which is not the same thing as random initialization.
nodes.boundary: Residual connections are covered in Chapter 49; neither mechanism represents knowledge already learned by the model.

nodes.label: Iteration / Optimizer Step / Epoch
nodes.description: An iteration is one loop cycle, an optimizer step is a parameter update, and an epoch usually traverses a finite dataset once.
explanation: A batch is a collection of samples processed together, and batch size is its sample count. An iteration usually means one execution of the training loop, although the code’s definition matters. An optimizer step is an actual parameter update. An epoch usually means one complete pass through a finite training dataset.

With 1,000 training samples and batches of 100, dropping no samples and updating once per batch gives ten batches and ten parameter updates per epoch. This is one epoch with ten update steps, not ten epochs. With streaming corpora or very large datasets, researchers may report optimizer steps or tokens processed rather than complete passes through the data.
nodes.boundary: Gradient accumulation or skipped updates means these counts are not interchangeable.

nodes.label: Kadane’s Algorithm
nodes.description: Maintain the largest nonempty subarray sum ending at the current position, choosing whether to extend the previous subarray or start a new one.
explanation: Maximum subarray sum can define the state as "the largest non-empty consecutive sum that must end at the current position". The new element is either connected to the previous interval or starts over; choose the larger value between the two, and then use the global answer to record the maximum value among all end points. The state only needs the previous value, so it can be squeezed into constant extra space.

For [-2,3,-1,4], the best sum ending at the final position comes from [3,-1,4]. If every value is negative, choose the largest negative value. Initializing the answer to zero would incorrectly allow an empty subarray.
nodes.boundary: An all-negative array still needs to return a negative number, which cannot be replaced by an empty interval of zero.

nodes.label: KL Divergence
nodes.description: Measure a directional discrepancy between probability distributions.
explanation: KL divergence measures a discrepancy between probability distributions. It can train a student model to match a teacher’s distribution or constrain a new policy from moving too far from a reference policy. KL divergence is generally asymmetric, so the direction of comparison matters. It is not a geometric distance or a direct measure of semantic similarity between answers. Cross-entropy, KL divergence and entropy are related, but explain which distributions are being compared rather than treating them as interchangeable losses.
nodes.boundary: KL divergence is not a symmetric distance, and input conventions depend on the implementation.

nodes.label: KNN / K-means
nodes.description: KNN predicts using labeled neighbors; K-means finds a specified number of centers in unlabeled data.
explanation: K-means fixes the number of clusters, alternates assignment to the nearest center with updates from cluster members, and suits compact groups under the chosen features and distance. It cannot fit arbitrary cluster shapes. K-means++ improves initialization by spreading centers apart, but does not guarantee a global optimum. Feature scales affect distance, so do not combine customer income and age without considering their units.
nodes.boundary: KNN is covered in Chapter 29. Similar names do not imply the same task.

nodes.label: KV Cache / FlashAttention
nodes.description: A KV cache reuses prefix keys and values; FlashAttention optimizes attention data movement and intermediate storage.
explanation: The KV cache stores keys and values already computed for processed tokens, avoiding repeated projections of the whole history. Each newly processed token still attends to relevant cached keys and values, so longer context still costs work. Prefix caching reuses computations across requests with a compatible shared prefix and model configuration. User-data isolation still matters: similar-looking text alone does not justify mixing caches.
nodes.boundary: Cache management, numerical quantization, and kernel optimization are different techniques.

nodes.label: Learning Rate
nodes.description: Control the overall scale of parameter updates, whose actual size also depends on gradients and optimizer state.
explanation: The learning rate controls the overall step size of optimizer updates. It measures neither how much knowledge has been learned nor how many epochs training has run. Imagine searching for low ground: the update direction tells you where to move, and the learning rate influences how far to move. Optimizers can also use historical gradients to scale individual parameter updates, so the learning rate is not the absolute change applied to every parameter.

If the stride length is too large, it may cross the favorable area at once, oscillate back and forth, and even cause numerical instability in training. Steps that are too small may result in slow improvement within a given budget. There is no single value that is best for all models, batch sizes, and optimizers. A smaller learning rate does not guarantee that the final generalization will be better, because the training budget, data, and other settings jointly affect the results.

Suppose two runs each train for ten epochs. With a learning rate that is too small, one may learn little in that time, while a suitable learning rate gives the other good validation performance. Equal epoch counts do not imply equal optimization progress. Conversely, unstable loss is not always caused by the learning rate: labels, the loss implementation or numerical precision may also be responsible.
nodes.boundary: The learning rate is neither the epoch count nor a fixed change to every weight.

nodes.label: Logit
nodes.description: In neural classification, a logit is usually a raw score before sigmoid or softmax.
explanation: In neural-network classification, a logit usually means a raw score before conversion to probability; it may be negative or exceed one. Sigmoid maps one score to a value between zero and one, often for whether a label holds. Softmax converts a set of scores to probabilities summing to one, distributing probability across mutually exclusive classes. These are output transformations, not complete learning algorithms or loss functions. A high probability does not ensure correctness, because calibration may be poor.
nodes.boundary: Scores may be negative or exceed one; they are not probabilities.

nodes.label: Loop Invariant
nodes.description: State a property that holds before the loop starts and is preserved by each iteration, then use it with the termination condition to establish correctness.
explanation: Two pointers are more than merely writing two indices. The positions must represent processed boundaries, current candidates, or traversals at different speeds, and each move must preserve all possible answers. A loop invariant describes a property that holds before and after every iteration. In Move Zeroes, the region before the write pointer always contains the nonzero elements retained in their original order; the read pointer keeps looking for the next element.

To preserve nonzero elements in place and in their original order, write them to the front and then fill the remainder with zeros. A swap-based version should not advance the write pointer when it reads zero. Linear time and constant auxiliary space permit more than one pass; two simple scans still meet those bounds.
nodes.boundary: Examples alone do not prove it; explain why every move preserves possible answers.

nodes.label: Loss / Objective / Metric
nodes.description: A loss supplies a training score, an objective may include additional constraints, and a metric measures task performance.
explanation: A loss scores model errors and is what training aims to improve. An objective function may also include requirements such as regularization. An evaluation metric indicates whether performance meets the task’s needs. The training objective and reported metric can differ: for example, train a purchase-probability predictor with BCE but assess precision or actual conversion outcomes after deployment. An optimizable loss gives training a direction, without guaranteeing complete alignment with the final business objective.
nodes.boundary: Reducing the training objective does not guarantee better business metrics.

nodes.label: Lower Bound / Upper Bound
nodes.description: In a sorted sequence, lower bound finds the first value at least the target, and upper bound finds the first value greater than it. Their difference counts occurrences.
explanation: Binary search relies on a monotonic true/false condition, rather than merely a sorted array. To find an insertion position, search for the first value greater than or equal to the target. With a half-open interval [left,right), initialize right to the array length. If the midpoint satisfies the condition, keep the left part including that midpoint; otherwise move left just past it. The search ends when left equals right, giving the boundary.

The invariant must preserve the desired boundary, which may equal the array length. Keep the termination and update rules consistent with either a half-open or a closed search interval. For fixed-width integers, computing the midpoint as left plus half of right-left can avoid the overflow of left+right.
nodes.boundary: Interval conventions and updates must agree. A boundary position does not itself prove the target exists.

nodes.label: Macro / Micro
nodes.description: Macro averaging computes each class metric and takes their equally weighted mean; micro averaging pools counts before computing the metric.
explanation: For multiclass or multilabel tasks, metrics can be calculated separately for each class and then averaged. Macro averaging gives every class equal weight, making problems in small classes easier to see. Weighted averaging uses weights such as class sample counts, so large classes can dominate. Micro averaging pools the counts first, then calculates the metric, emphasizing overall sample-level performance. All three scores may be called F1 but differ, so comparisons must specify the averaging method.
nodes.boundary: Class-frequency-weighted averaging is a separate convention affected by class sample counts.

nodes.label: Microbatch / Gradient Accumulation
nodes.description: Run forward and backward passes on several small batches, then update once after accumulating gradients to reduce peak activation storage.
explanation: When GPU memory cannot fit many samples at once, split them into microbatches, run forward and backward passes separately, accumulate their gradients and then update. For example, compute gradients after each microbatch but update parameters only after four microbatches: four iterations correspond to one optimizer step. This gives a larger effective batch, but is not always exactly equivalent to one large batch. BatchNorm statistics, for example, can differ. Gradient accumulation does not mean parameters change after every microbatch.
nodes.boundary: Partial final batches, loss normalization, and BatchNorm can affect equivalence to a large batch.

nodes.label: Mixed Precision / Loss Scaling
nodes.description: Use different numerical precisions for operations; loss scaling helps some low-precision gradients remain representable.
explanation: These names denote floating-point formats. Lower precision generally saves memory and can accelerate computation on supported hardware, but the numerical range and resolution differ. BF16 has an exponent range similar to FP32 but lower precision; FP16 has a narrower representable range. Mixed precision uses different formats for different operations, often retaining higher precision for sensitive calculations. It does not simply make all numbers smaller, and does not guarantee equal speedups on every device.
nodes.boundary: Unscaling and optimizer updates must occur at the correct accumulation boundaries.

nodes.label: Monotonic Deque
nodes.description: Maintain candidate indices for window extrema in a deque and remove expired candidates from the front.
explanation: For a sliding-window maximum, a deque stores indices in nonincreasing order of their values. When a new value arrives, remove indices from the back while their values are no greater: the new value is at least as large and expires later. Remove the front index when it leaves the window. The remaining front gives the current maximum.

For example, the window sweeps through one, three, and two. When three enters, one can be eliminated, but two cannot eliminate three. Each index can enter and exit the queue once at most, so the amortized time is linear. Use a queue that supports constant-time operations on both ends; deleting the head of an ordinary array in some languages will move elements, and it cannot be claimed that the implementation is still linear.
nodes.boundary: This differs from a monotonic stack. Linear-time array-front deletion can degrade the implementation.

nodes.label: Monotonic Stack
nodes.description: Store unresolved candidates and pop those whose answers become determined when a new element arrives.
explanation: Daily Temperatures maintains a stack of indices with nonincreasing temperatures. When a warmer temperature arrives, repeatedly pop indices; the difference between the current index and the popped index is the waiting time. The stack contains positions whose answers are unresolved, and popped positions need no further work. Each index is pushed and popped once, giving linear total work by amortized analysis. Equal temperature is not warmer, so it must not resolve an earlier position.
nodes.boundary: Linear total work follows because each item enters and leaves at most once. Specify comparisons for equal values.

nodes.label: MSE / MAE / RMSE
nodes.description: MSE emphasizes large errors; MAE is more robust to extreme residuals; RMSE has the same units as the target.
explanation: MSE, mean squared error, is common in continuous-value prediction and penalizes large errors strongly. MAE, mean absolute error, measures the magnitude of deviations from the true value and is less sensitive to extreme errors. RMSE is the square root of MSE and has the same units as the target. For temperature predictions, an error in degrees is easier to interpret than one in squared degrees. These losses and metrics can be used with other suitable models, not only linear regression.
nodes.boundary: Account for the target’s units and the different penalties on large errors when choosing or comparing these measures.

nodes.label: Multi-source BFS
nodes.description: Initialize several sources at distance zero and expand by BFS layers to find earliest arrival in an equal-weight graph.
explanation: For Rotting Oranges, enqueue all initially rotten cells at time zero. One BFS level represents one minute; the first time a fresh orange is reached is its rotting time. Track the number of fresh oranges remaining. If any remain after traversal, they are unreachable. With no fresh oranges initially, the answer is zero.

The earliest arrival conclusion of BFS relies on each propagation edge taking the same time. If the propagation time of different grids is different, methods such as weighted shortest path must be considered, and the number of layers cannot be directly regarded as time.
nodes.boundary: With unequal edge travel times, layer count need not equal shortest travel time.

nodes.label: NaN / Inf / OOM
nodes.description: NaN and Inf indicate numerical anomalies; OOM indicates insufficient memory.
explanation: Loss scaling amplifies the loss in some mixed-precision training so that small gradients remain representable, then compensates before updating. NaN denotes an invalid numeric value; Inf denotes infinity, for example after overflow. These can arise from division by zero, extreme scores or unstable operations. OOM means out of memory, not exploding gradients. For OOM, inspect batch size, sequence length, saved activations and model size. For NaN, inspect numerical values and data first.
nodes.boundary: Separate numerical diagnosis from memory diagnosis first.

nodes.label: Off-policy / Offline RL
nodes.description: Off-policy methods can learn a target policy from data generated by another policy; offline RL learns from a fixed dataset.
explanation: Offline RL trains on a fixed collection of interactions without gathering new experience from the environment during training. It can overestimate actions poorly covered by the dataset. CQL addresses this with conservative value estimation; IQL fits values and extracts a policy while limiting dependence on evaluating actions outside the data. Neither creates missing coverage. Offline evaluation is also an imperfect substitute for safe, controlled real-world validation.
nodes.boundary: An off-policy algorithm can also collect new experience continuously online.

nodes.label: Parameter / Hyperparameter
nodes.description: Parameters are obtained by fitting, and hyperparameters usually control the model structure or training method.
explanation: Weights and biases are learnable model values; “parameter” is the general category. Learning rate, batch size, and maximum tree depth are usually hyperparameters controlling the model or training, rather than weights directly fitted by ordinary training. A bias term is not the statistical bias in the bias–variance tradeoff or social bias. The same word has different meanings: first determine whether the discussion concerns model structure, statistical error, or fairness.
nodes.boundary: Learning rate and batch size are usually hyperparameters.

nodes.label: PCA — Principal Component Analysis
nodes.description: Find orthogonal directions of maximum variance, usually after centering the data, to construct a lower-dimensional linear representation.
explanation: PCA finds linear directions of greatest variation, retaining as much overall variation as possible with fewer coordinates. It supports compression, denoising, and preprocessing, but greatest variance is not necessarily most predictive: class differences may lie in low-variance directions. Standard PCA uses no supervised labels and does not guarantee preservation of classification-relevant information. Input scales influence results; whether to standardize depends on the task.
nodes.boundary: High-variance directions need not be the most useful for classification.

nodes.label: PID / MPC
nodes.description: PID uses feedback from error and its history or changes; MPC repeatedly plans under a model and constraints.
explanation: PID adjusts control using current error, accumulated error and the rate of error change to track a desired state. The proportional term responds to deviation, the integral term handles persistent offset, and the derivative term can provide damping. Noise, delay and tuning affect stability. PID is not learned from large video datasets, but is useful in many stabilization tasks.
nodes.boundary: The prediction horizon may differ from the executed horizon.

nodes.label: Postorder DP
nodes.description: Compute subtree summaries first, then form the value returned to the parent or a global candidate answer.
explanation: Maximum depth returns the larger child depth plus one to the parent. Diameter updates a global answer at each node using the sum of its left and right depths, but returns only a one-sided depth. Maximum Path Sum needs the same distinction: a node can join both sides when updating the global answer, but a path passed to its parent can extend along only one side and cannot branch.

When calculating the maximum path sum, negative subtree contributions are not required, but negative numbers should be allowed in the global answer, otherwise a fully negative tree will return zero by mistake. The diameter is usually calculated by the number of edges, and the depth is usually calculated by the number of nodes. The initialization and increment must be consistent with the definition.
nodes.boundary: A one-sided path passed upward differs from a candidate joining both sides at the current node.

nodes.label: PPO / SAC / TD3
nodes.description: PPO typically clips a policy surrogate objective, SAC incorporates entropy regularization, and TD3 reduces overestimation in continuous-action actor–critic learning.
explanation: TRPO uses a trust-region approach to constrain policy changes and avoid destroying existing behavior in one update. PPO pursues similar stability through easier-to-implement objectives, such as clipping or penalties. It commonly performs several updates on a newly collected batch of interactions before gathering fresh data. PPO controls update incentives; it does not enforce the same maximum change on every parameter or guarantee that a policy never moves too far.
nodes.boundary: Clipping the PPO objective differs from clipping gradients and does not impose a hard bound on every policy change.

nodes.label: Precision
nodes.description: Among examples predicted positive, the fraction that are actually positive: TP/(TP+FP).
explanation: Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.
nodes.boundary: The denominator counts predicted positives, not actual positives. Precision is undefined when no examples are predicted positive unless a reporting convention is specified.

nodes.label: Prefix Sum
nodes.description: Store cumulative sums at boundaries and obtain a range sum by subtracting two prefixes.
explanation: Define the prefix sum P such that the sum of the first zero elements is zero. The sum of a segment is k, which is equivalent to the current prefix sum minus an earlier prefix sum equal to k. Therefore, when scanning the current prefix P, check how many times P minus k has appeared before, then accumulate the answer, and finally record the current P. The occurrence of the zero prefix must be recorded once at the beginning to count the interval starting from the beginning of the array.

For example, one, negative one, one, the target is one. The three legal intervals come from two single elements and the entire array; the prefix frequency can count the contribution of repeated prefixes. The hash table must save the number of times, not just whether it exists. Recording the current prefix first and then querying will incorrectly include empty intervals when k is zero.
nodes.boundary: Counting often needs prefix frequencies and an initial zero prefix. Tree paths also need state undo on return.

nodes.label: Q-learning / SARSA
nodes.description: Q-learning forms updates using a greedy target action; SARSA uses the next action actually taken.
explanation: Classic Q-learning uses the estimated value of the best next-state action in its target, even when exploration actually selects another action. SARSA uses the value of the action actually selected next under the behavior policy. This illustrates off-policy versus on-policy learning: the relationship between the target policy and the policy collecting data. Off-policy does not mean offline; an off-policy algorithm can collect new data while learning.
nodes.boundary: They relate the behavior policy and target policy differently.

nodes.label: Quickselect / Top K
nodes.description: Quickselect recurses or iterates only into the partition containing the target rank. A bounded heap can instead maintain the current Top K in a stream.
explanation: If you want to find the kth largest value, you don't have to sort the entire array. Maintain a min-heap with a size of at most k. The top of the heap is the minimum value among the current retainers, which is the elimination threshold. It is worth replacing only if the new value exceeds the threshold. After scanning, the top of the heap will be the kth largest. The frequencies of the top k high-frequency elements are first counted, and then the same selection is made according to the frequency. The ranking object changes from the numerical value to the frequency of the key.

The heap only guarantees the extreme value at the top of the heap, and does not guarantee the overall ordering of the internal array. Here, the kth largest number of elements is counted, and repeated values still account for multiple rankings; the top k high-frequency objects are different keys and must be distinguished.
nodes.boundary: Quickselect usually modifies input. Randomized versions have expected linear but worst-case quadratic time.

nodes.label: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
nodes.description: Retrieve relevant material, then have a generative model answer using it.
nodes.boundary: Retrieval does not guarantee a correct answer or sufficient evidence.

nodes.label: Random Forest
nodes.description: Train trees using random sample selection and candidate features, then aggregate their predictions.
explanation: Random forests predict with many trees. Classic training gives each tree a different bootstrap sample and limits each split to a random feature subset. This second randomness is crucial: if one strong feature always dominates the top split, trees become similar; limiting candidates lets them explore different rules.

Regression usually averages tree values; classification may vote or average class probabilities depending on implementation. Different perspectives reduce a single tree's high variance. They cannot recover information every tree lacks, nor guarantee freedom from overfitting.
nodes.boundary: Random forests mainly reduce variance; they do not guarantee freedom from overfitting.

nodes.label: Recall
nodes.description: Among actual positive examples, the fraction predicted positive: TP/(TP+FN). Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.
explanation: Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.
nodes.boundary: Improving recall does not mean false positives are necessarily acceptable.

nodes.label: Regularization
nodes.description: Use penalties or training constraints to limit reliance on details specific to training data.
nodes.boundary: Excessive regularization can suppress real signal.

nodes.label: Replication / Sharding
nodes.description: Replication stores copies of the same data; sharding partitions data across nodes.
nodes.boundary: The number of copies and the way data is divided solve different problems.

nodes.label: ROC AUC / PR AUC
nodes.description: ROC curves summarize true- and false-positive rates; PR curves summarize precision and recall as a threshold varies.
nodes.boundary: Average precision and trapezoidal area under a PR curve need not be identical.

nodes.label: Sample / Feature / Label
nodes.description: A sample is a learning instance, features are available inputs, and a label is a supervised target.
explanation: A sample is one example, such as an order. A feature is information available for prediction, such as price or a user's previous view count. A label is a supervised answer, such as whether the order was later canceled. Target is a broader term for the value or content the model is trained to predict or reconstruct: a class, number, next text segment, or image. Labels need not be manually annotated: next-word prediction gets its answers from the text itself. Distinguish answers available during training from information available at prediction time. If an answer unavailable at prediction time enters the input during training or evaluation, it causes data leakage.
nodes.boundary: Information unavailable at prediction time causes leakage if included among features.

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.description: Rules for changing the learning rate based on training progress or validation performance.
explanation: A learning-rate scheduler specifies how the learning rate changes. Step decay reduces it at specified points; exponential decay reduces it proportionally; cosine annealing follows a smooth cosine curve. ReduceLROnPlateau monitors a metric and lowers the rate when improvement stalls. These rules respond to either a fixed schedule or observed performance. Choose with the total training duration and the need for finer updates near the end in mind.
nodes.boundary: Specify whether the schedule advances with optimizer updates, iterations, epochs, or validation checks.

nodes.label: SFT / LoRA / QLoRA
nodes.description: SFT defines a supervised training stage and objective; LoRA and QLoRA are adaptation methods with parameter and memory implications.
explanation: Pretraining learns general patterns from large-scale data. Continued pretraining applies similar objectives to an existing model, often with additional domain data. SFT uses input–expected-response pairs to shape task behavior. These stages can all update parameters but differ in data format and objective. Adding documents does not always require fine-tuning: retrieval can also supply frequently updated knowledge with citations.
nodes.boundary: A training stage and a parameter-efficient adaptation method describe different aspects.

nodes.label: SGD / Momentum
nodes.description: SGD uses sampled gradients; momentum incorporates a history of update directions.
explanation: Full-batch gradient descent uses all training samples to compute an update direction. This gives a less noisy direction but is expensive for large datasets. Strictly, stochastic gradient descent can mean using one sample per update, although modern training commonly uses SGD to mean minibatch training. Minibatches give noisier directions but allow more frequent updates and hardware parallelism. Stochastic gradients are estimates from sampled data, not arbitrary changes to parameters.
nodes.boundary: In modern use, SGD often means the minibatch version.

nodes.label: Sigmoid
nodes.description: Map a real-valued score into the interval between zero and one, often for a binary-label probability.
explanation: In neural-network classification, a logit usually means a raw score before conversion to probability; it may be negative or exceed one. Sigmoid maps one score to a value between zero and one, often for whether a label holds. Softmax converts a set of scores to probabilities summing to one, distributing probability across mutually exclusive classes. These are output transformations, not complete learning algorithms or loss functions. A high probability does not ensure correctness, because calibration may be poor.
nodes.boundary: Do not usually apply sigmoid before BCEWithLogitsLoss.

nodes.label: Sliding Window
nodes.description: Maintain a contiguous interval and incremental state such as frequencies, searching through expansion and contraction.
explanation: The sliding window maintains a contiguous interval, allowing the right end to incorporate new elements, the left end to remove old elements, and incrementally update status such as frequency. First define when the current range is legal, and then decide when to shrink. In the longest substring without repeated characters, once a new character causes repetition, the window will continue to be narrowed until there are no more repetitions, and then the maximum length will be updated.

For example, on the second b in abba, move left past both the leading a and the first b; removing just one character is insufficient. If using last-seen indices, set left to the maximum of its current value and the repeated character’s previous index plus one. This prevents left from moving backward at the final a.
nodes.boundary: With negative values, interval sums are not monotonic under expansion; positive-array window rules do not apply unchanged.

nodes.label: Softmax
nodes.description: Convert a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to one.
explanation: In neural-network classification, a logit usually means a raw score before conversion to probability; it may be negative or exceed one. Sigmoid maps one score to a value between zero and one, often for whether a label holds. Softmax converts a set of scores to probabilities summing to one, distributing probability across mutually exclusive classes. These are output transformations, not complete learning algorithms or loss functions. A high probability does not ensure correctness, because calibration may be poor.
nodes.boundary: Independent multilabel outputs do not require mutually exclusive softmax merely because many labels exist.

nodes.label: Tensor / Shape / Axis
nodes.description: A tensor organizes multidimensional data, its shape lists axis sizes, and an axis identifies a direction of organization or computation.
explanation: For now, think of a tensor as a multidimensional array. Its shape gives its size along each direction; an axis identifies a direction of organization or computation. A color-image batch can have sample, channel, height, and width axes. “Dimension” may mean the number of axes or the size of one axis, so context matters. Embedding dimension usually means components per vector, not dataset sample count. Shape mismatches concern data alignment, not necessarily a flaw in the algorithm's principle.
nodes.boundary: “Dimension” may mean the number of axes or the size of one axis; check context.

nodes.label: Threshold
nodes.description: Turn a probability or score into a hard classification decision using a cutoff.
explanation: A classification threshold must still be chosen after predicting probabilities. Raising it usually produces fewer positive predictions but may miss more actual positives. The confusion matrix distinguishes true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Sensitivity usually means recall, or the true positive rate. Specificity measures the proportion of actual negatives correctly excluded. These measure different aspects of performance and should be discussed in terms of missed detections and false alarms.
nodes.boundary: Choose thresholds on validation data according to false-positive and false-negative costs.

nodes.label: Token / Embedding
nodes.description: A token is a discrete processing unit; an embedding maps such units to learnable vectors.
nodes.boundary: A token need not correspond to one character or one word.

nodes.label: Topological Sort
nodes.description: Order vertices to satisfy precedence constraints in a directed acyclic graph.
explanation: For Course Schedule, encode prerequisites as directed edges. Enqueue every zero-in-degree vertex, process it, and decrement its successors’ in-degrees. Enqueue a successor when its in-degree reaches zero. All courses are feasible exactly when all vertices are processed; otherwise the remaining graph contains a directed cycle. Include isolated courses in the total.

A DFS alternative uses visitation colors. Encountering a vertex that is still on the active recursion path reveals a directed cycle; encountering a fully processed vertex does not. A topological order exists only for a DAG. Ordinary BFS without dependency bookkeeping does not provide this test.
nodes.boundary: If the in-degree algorithm cannot process every vertex, a directed cycle exists. Encountering a previously visited vertex alone is insufficient evidence.

nodes.label: Train / Eval / No Grad
nodes.description: Train and eval modes change the behavior of certain layers; no_grad controls gradient recording.
explanation: Training and evaluation modes control the behavior of layers such as Dropout and BatchNorm. Disabling gradient recording controls whether the information needed for backpropagation is recorded. These are separate: switching to evaluation mode does not disable every gradient, and disabling gradients does not change Dropout’s training behavior. Set both correctly during evaluation or deployment for stable behavior and efficient resource use.
nodes.boundary: Evaluation mode and disabling gradients do not replace one another.

nodes.label: Transaction / ACID
nodes.description: Treat a set of operations as a logical unit and discuss atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.
nodes.boundary: Different isolation levels have different observable behaviors during concurrency.

nodes.label: Two Pointers
nodes.description: Assign two positions boundary or candidate roles and eliminate repeated enumeration through safe movement.
explanation: Two pointers are more than merely writing two indices. The positions must represent processed boundaries, current candidates, or traversals at different speeds, and each move must preserve all possible answers. A loop invariant describes a property that holds before and after every iteration. In Move Zeroes, the region before the write pointer always contains the nonzero elements retained in their original order; the read pointer keeps looking for the next element.

To preserve nonzero elements in place and in their original order, write them to the front and then fill the remainder with zeros. A swap-based version should not advance the write pointer when it reads zero. Linear time and constant auxiliary space permit more than one pass; two simple scans still meet those bounds.
nodes.boundary: Two indices are not a proof; justify moves using ordering, bounds, or another elimination argument.

nodes.label: VAE / GAN / Diffusion
nodes.description: Learn data distribution through different training objectives and generation processes.
explanation: A VAE maps observations through an encoder to a probability distribution over latent variables, then reconstructs or generates samples with a decoder. Training combines reconstruction with constraints on the latent distribution, making sampling from a simple prior useful. The distinguishing feature is probabilistic latent-variable modeling, not merely dimensionality reduction. Latent variables can be ignored in some settings, so check what information the model actually uses.
nodes.boundary: Just because they can all generate images does not mean that the training mechanisms are the same.

nodes.label: VLA — Vision-Language-Action Model
nodes.description: Produce executable actions conditioned on vision and language.
nodes.boundary: A policy using vision alone is not necessarily a vision-language-action model.

nodes.label: Warmup / Warm Start
nodes.description: Warmup gradually raises the learning rate at the start; a warm start begins from an existing model or state.
explanation: Warmup first uses a smaller learning rate at the beginning of training, and then gradually increases it to the target level.
