Its purpose is to get training off to a smoother start, rather than letting the GPU heat up first. Then other scheduling methods are usually added. Not all models must use warmup; warmup that is too long can also eat up the effective training budget. Warmup is different from warm start: the latter usually refers to continuing from an existing model or state, rather than starting over from random initialization.
nodes.boundary: They describe different mechanisms and can be used together.

nodes.label: Weight Decay
nodes.description: Shrink weights during parameter updates to regularize the model.
explanation: Weight decay discourages excessively large weights. AdamW decouples it from Adam’s adaptive gradient scaling instead of treating it as an ordinary gradient term. For basic SGD, L2 regularization and weight decay can be equivalent under common conditions; that equivalence does not carry over directly to adaptive optimizers. In an interview, explain that the W in AdamW refers to decoupled weight decay, rather than describing it simply as faster Adam.
nodes.boundary: Weight decay differs from learning-rate decay; equivalence to an L2 penalty depends on the optimizer.

nodes.label: World Model
nodes.description: Model how an environment’s state or latent representation evolves under actions to support prediction and decision-making.
nodes.boundary: Realistic video does not automatically provide reliable action-conditioned prediction or control.

nodes.label: Zero Grad / Detach
nodes.description: zero_grad clears accumulated gradients; detach cuts a path through which gradients would propagate.
explanation: Some frameworks accumulate new gradients onto existing ones by default, so clear gradients at the appropriate update boundaries. Failing to clear them can count old gradients again; clearing them too early defeats intended accumulation. Detach and stop-gradient operations block gradient propagation along a path, for example in target networks, teacher branches or unnecessary computation graphs. Detaching does not necessarily copy the underlying data and does not freeze the entire model.
nodes.boundary: detach does not automatically copy storage or freeze the entire model.

nodes.label: Stack
nodes.description: Store unfinished contexts in last-in, first-out order for bracket matching, restoring earlier minima, or decoding nested expressions.
nodes.boundary: An ordinary stack expresses nesting; a monotonic stack additionally orders candidate values.

nodes.label: Greedy
nodes.description: Build solutions through provably safe choices or expansions of a reachable boundary.
nodes.boundary: A locally attractive choice need not be globally correct; justify it through elimination or exchange.

nodes.label: Complexity
nodes.description: Analyze time, auxiliary storage, and output cost separately, distinguishing expected, amortized, and worst-case bounds.
nodes.boundary: Loop nesting alone does not determine complexity; include data-structure operations and output size.

nodes.label: Recursion
nodes.description: Define the subproblem each call solves, its return value, and its base cases, then organize recursive calls.
nodes.boundary: Tree return values, search-path state, and backtracking undo have different semantics.

nodes.label: Data Structures
nodes.description: Choose an organization of information according to the main operations and their access, update, ordering, and connectivity costs.
nodes.boundary: A data structure supplies operations rather than determining the entire task’s algorithm.

nodes.label: Heap
nodes.description: Support efficient access to a minimum or maximum, with insertion and removal, for Top K, merging, or streaming statistics.
nodes.boundary: A heap is not totally ordered; its underlying array is not a sorted result.

nodes.label: Trie
nodes.description: Share character paths to support word and prefix lookup, using terminal markers to distinguish complete words.
nodes.boundary: Storage depends on created nodes and child representations. Merely stating linear operation time is incomplete.

nodes.label: Graph Algorithms
nodes.description: Convert connections, reachability, shortest paths and sequential dependencies into nodes, edges and corresponding traversal or optimization problems.
nodes.boundary: Whether the graph is directed, whether the edge weights are non-negative, and whether the weights are equal will change the applicable algorithm.

nodes.label: Operating System
nodes.description: Manage program execution, memory, scheduling and synchronization to allow limited resources to serve multiple tasks.
nodes.boundary: Concurrency and parallelism describe task progress and execution; blocking and asynchrony describe waiting and control flow.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.description: Understand naming, transport, protocols, congestion, caching, and load distribution along the request path.
nodes.boundary: Latency and throughput are different indicators, and service reliability also involves retries and idempotence.

nodes.label: Consensus
nodes.description: Have multiple nodes agree on log or state progress under specified communication and failure constraints.
nodes.boundary: Copying data alone does not guarantee agreement under arbitrary failures.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.description: Store reusable data or results to avoid repeated work, while managing capacity, validity, and replacement.
nodes.boundary: LRU decides which entry to evict; a KV cache reuses attention keys and values. They operate on different data and constraints.

nodes.label: Feature Engineering
nodes.description: Turn raw data into usable input for tasks and estimate processing statistics within the correct training partitions.
nodes.boundary: Preprocessing, feature selection, and target encoding can all introduce leakage.

nodes.label: Linear Models
nodes.description: Use linear combinations of features, possibly with basis expansions, link functions, and regularization, to model targets.
nodes.boundary: Logistic regression usually models classification probabilities; “regression” in its name does not restrict outputs to continuous targets.

nodes.label: Decision Tree
nodes.description: Split data through target-related feature conditions and form predictions at leaves.
nodes.boundary: Deep trees can be unstable. Complexity control and ensemble methods address this in different ways.

nodes.label: Clustering
nodes.description: Characterize the grouping structure of unlabeled data based on distance, density, or probability models.
nodes.boundary: Clusters need not match real-world categories. Distance scales, density assumptions, and cluster shapes affect the grouping.

nodes.label: Anomaly Detection
nodes.description: Construct anomaly scores based on isolation, local density, boundaries, or model error.
nodes.boundary: The anomaly score does not automatically equal the calibrated anomaly probability.

nodes.label: Time Series
nodes.description: Model evolving data through temporal dependencies, trends, error structures, or hidden states.
nodes.boundary: Validation must respect time order; future information cannot enter past predictions.

nodes.label: Causality
nodes.description: Distinguish predictive association from intervention effects, using experiments, assumptions, and uncertainty to support conclusions.
nodes.boundary: Feature importance and quality of fit alone do not prove causality.

nodes.label: Neural Network
nodes.description: Compose parameterized transformations to learn representations, usually by optimizing a training objective with gradients.
nodes.boundary: Network structure, loss function, optimization method and evaluation criteria are at different levels.

nodes.label: CNN — Convolutional Neural Network
nodes.description: Use local connections and shared weights to process structured data such as images; residual connections can help organize deeper networks.
nodes.boundary: Local connectivity and weight sharing are inductive biases. They do not guarantee invariance to transformations or better performance on every task.

nodes.label: RNN — Recurrent Neural Network
nodes.description: Summarize history in a hidden state updated along a sequence; gating mechanisms regulate information retention.
nodes.boundary: Sequence length, gradient propagation, and parallelization constraints jointly affect suitability.

nodes.label: MLOps
nodes.description: Connect training, versioning, deployment, and production monitoring into a maintainable engineering process.
nodes.boundary: Better offline metrics do not guarantee favorable production distributions or business outcomes.

nodes.label: Multimodal Representation
nodes.description: Learn representations and correspondences across text, images, speech and other data, serving retrieval and conditional generation.
nodes.boundary: Embedding similarity, cross-modal understanding, and reliable action are distinct evaluation goals.

nodes.label: Bellman Equations
nodes.description: Relate immediate rewards to subsequent values to organize long-term decision learning, distinguishing evaluation from control.
nodes.boundary: Value depends on the policy, discount, and task; single-step rewards alone are insufficient for comparison.

nodes.label: Policy Gradient
nodes.description: Improve the action policy directly, often using value estimates to construct learning signals.
nodes.boundary: Constraints in a policy objective differ from gradient clipping.

nodes.label: Imitation Learning
nodes.description: Learn actions or policies from expert demonstrations while considering distribution shift and interactive feedback.
nodes.boundary: Behavior cloning may fit demonstrations without keeping its own rollout states within the demonstration distribution.

nodes.label: Motion Planning
nodes.description: Find collision-free paths or feasible trajectories through a robot’s configuration or state space.
nodes.boundary: Geometric paths, dynamic constraints, state estimation, and feedback control address different parts of robot motion.

nodes.label: Disjoint-set Union
nodes.description: Maintain disjoint sets through representatives, supporting connectivity tests and merging.
nodes.boundary: Ordinary DSU mainly handles added connections. Path compression changes tree shape without changing set membership.

nodes.label: 0-1 BFS
nodes.description: Use a deque to find shortest paths when every edge weight is 0 or 1.
nodes.boundary: Relax whenever distance improves; first enqueueing does not make a distance final.

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford
nodes.description: Use repeated relaxation to handle negative edges and identify effects of negative cycles reachable from the source.
nodes.boundary: A negative cycle unreachable from the source does not invalidate all that source’s results.

nodes.label: Fenwick Tree
nodes.description: Support point increments and prefix sums through binary-sized blocks.
nodes.boundary: The one-based update interface excludes index 0; obtain range sums by subtracting prefixes.

nodes.label: Segment Tree
nodes.description: Maintain mergeable interval summaries hierarchically and propagate range updates when needed.
nodes.boundary: Lazy-tag composition order and summary updates must match the operation.

nodes.label: Difference Array
nodes.description: Represent batched range additions as endpoint changes, then reconstruct values by prefix accumulation.
nodes.boundary: Basic difference arrays suit offline reconstruction; online queries usually require another structure.

nodes.label: KMP Prefix Function
nodes.description: Reuse the matched segment’s proper-prefix/suffix information after a mismatch.
nodes.boundary: Prefix-function values are lengths. Specify overlap handling after matches and the empty-pattern convention.

nodes.label: Aho-Corasick
nodes.description: Match multiple patterns using trie failure links and output relationships.
nodes.boundary: State the transition implementation and include the actual number of reported matches in complexity.

nodes.label: LIS Tails
nodes.description: Store the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length and update strict-LIS length with binary search.
nodes.boundary: tails need not itself be a subsequence of the input. Reconstruction requires additional predecessor information.

nodes.label: Weighted Interval Scheduling
nodes.description: Sort tasks by finish time and combine each selection with the optimum at its compatible predecessor.
nodes.boundary: Maximizing task count differs from maximizing reward; earliest-finish greedy does not apply unconditionally.

nodes.label: Interval DP
nodes.description: Define subproblems on contiguous intervals and solve them from shorter to longer intervals, often by enumerating a final split or operation.
nodes.boundary: The task determines the merge cost; one interval template does not fit every problem.

nodes.label: Bitmask DP
nodes.description: Encode a small set in the state, explicitly retaining visited vertices and the current endpoint when needed.
nodes.boundary: Bitmasks do not remove the exponential state count, and language integer widths are limited.

nodes.label: Binary Search on the Answer
nodes.description: Find an optimal boundary using a monotonic feasibility test on candidate answers.
nodes.boundary: Prove any greedy feasibility test independently; constraints such as negative values can change the argument.

nodes.label: Reservoir Sampling
nodes.description: Sample uniformly from a stream of unknown final length using fixed storage.
nodes.boundary: Correct probabilities depend on uniform-index bounds and the definition of a sampling unit.

nodes.label: Bloom Filter
nodes.description: Use a bit array and several hash positions for membership filtering that permits false positives.
nodes.boundary: Standard insert-only use has no false negatives. Directly clearing shared bits is not safe deletion.

nodes.label: Amortized Analysis
nodes.description: Bound the total cost of an operation sequence and distribute it across operations.
nodes.boundary: Amortized analysis is not expected analysis over random inputs and does not make every operation cheap.

nodes.label: Exact Decimal Arithmetic / Minor Units
nodes.description: A fixed-point representation stores an integer coefficient and an explicit decimal scale. Conversion must also respect the allowed increments of the target API operation.
explanation: Represent a value as m/10^s. To increase the scale, multiply m by a power of ten. To reduce it without rounding, require the discarded digits to be zero. Decimal-string operations can implement this conversion without a binary floating-point intermediate.

Keep the representation scale separate from the allowed amount quantum. Stripe represents ISK with two decimal places but permits only whole-ISK charges; HUF and TWD manual payouts similarly require minor-unit integers divisible by 100.
nodes.boundary: Representation scale and allowed increments can differ by operation. Input grammar, precision, and divisibility need separate checks. Integer storage must be wide enough; arbitrary-precision arithmetic does not have constant cost for unbounded digit counts.

nodes.label: Cryptographic Hashes / Streaming Digests
nodes.description: A cryptographic hash maps bytes to a fixed-size digest. Incremental hashing processes a byte stream in pieces while preserving the digest of their concatenation.
explanation: Dropbox content_hash first hashes each 4,194,304-byte block with SHA-256, then hashes the concatenation of the raw 32-byte block digests. Only the final digest is encoded as hexadecimal. Transport chunk boundaries do not change the fixed block boundaries.

Keep one inner hash context, one outer context, and a block-byte counter. Finalize every full block and any remaining nonempty block. An empty file contributes no inner block; an exact block multiple must not append an empty block.
nodes.boundary: Dropbox content_hash differs from SHA-256 applied directly to the file. Hash-table indexing, content identification, and authentication have different requirements. Digest equality is subject to collision assumptions and does not by itself authenticate a sender.

nodes.label: Unicode Grapheme Clusters / UTF-8
nodes.description: A user-perceived character, a Unicode scalar, and an encoded byte are different units. Swift Character represents an extended grapheme cluster; UTF-8 measures its encoded bytes.
explanation: The decomposed string e followed by a combining acute accent contains two Unicode scalars but one grapheme cluster and three UTF-8 bytes. A multi-scalar emoji can also form one Character.

For a byte-limited prefix that preserves characters, visit whole grapheme clusters in order and accumulate each cluster's UTF-8 length. Stop before the next cluster would exceed the budget. Segmentation should use a Unicode-aware library rather than byte slicing.
nodes.boundary: Counting characters does not give a byte length. Canonically equivalent text can have different byte sequences. The segmentation version and normalization policy are part of an interoperable text-processing contract.

nodes.label: Backpressure / Subscriber Demand
nodes.description: Backpressure lets a consumer signal how much work it can accept. In Combine, subscriber demand limits how many elements a subscription may deliver.
explanation: With finite demand, each delivered element consumes one credit. Explicit requests and the additional demand returned by receive add credits; returning none adds zero and does not cancel existing demand.

A PassthroughSubject does not buffer values for later demand. With one subscriber and zero demand, a sent value is dropped for that subscriber. Other publishers and buffering operators can have different policies.
nodes.boundary: Demand limits deliveries rather than elapsed-time request rate. Unlimited demand, cancellation, reentrant sends, multiple subscribers, and completion require their own protocol rules.

nodes.label: Max-min Fairness / Water Filling
nodes.description: Max-min allocation protects smaller unsatisfied allocations before increasing larger ones. For one divisible resource with equal weights and demand caps, progressive water filling computes the allocation.
explanation: For capacity C >= 0 and demands d_i >= 0, allocate x_i = min(d_i, lambda), choosing a common water level so the total is min(C, sum d_i). A demand-capped consumer leaves the sharing set when its cap is reached.

Sort demands, satisfy the smallest cap when it is no greater than the remaining equal share, then divide the remaining capacity equally among active consumers. Sorting costs O(n log(n + 1)) time; the subsequent scan is linear.
nodes.boundary: This formula assumes equal weights and one divisible resource, without reservations, placement constraints, or indivisible jobs. Peloton's hierarchical, weighted, multi-resource scheduler has additional policies.

nodes.label: Adaptive Concurrency / Queue Estimation
nodes.description: An adaptive concurrency limiter changes the allowed number of in-flight requests using observed service behavior. Latency relative to an unloaded baseline can estimate queue buildup.
explanation: For limit L, baseline latency R0, and sample latency R >= R0 > 0, Netflix's pinned Vegas implementation estimates queue size as ceil(L(1 - R0/R)). Its update also considers drops, utilization, configured thresholds, bounds, and smoothing.

The exercise fixes the baseline and policy to make each transition checkable. The full implementation also primes the baseline and periodically probes it; those branches can skip a normal limit update.
nodes.boundary: The queue estimate is a model, not a measured count of waiting requests. A concurrency cap is distinct from a request-rate quota. This pinned open-source implementation does not establish Netflix's current production configuration.

nodes.label: SQL Aggregation / Join Cardinality
nodes.description: SQL aggregates summarize rows after filtering and joining. Correct counts depend on the unit being counted and the number of rows each join produces.
explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(expression) ignores NULL values, and COUNT(DISTINCT expression) counts distinct nonnull values. A left join creates a NULL-filled row for an unmatched parent; a one-to-many join can repeat each parent's values.

Group by stable identifiers when different entities can share a name. To return every maximum, compare each result with the maximum aggregate rather than selecting one arbitrary row. Compute percentages with the intended denominator and real-valued division; use ORDER BY when output order matters.
nodes.boundary: SQL does not promise row order without ORDER BY. Empty groups, NULL, duplicate join matches, and tied maxima need explicit contracts. Logical query semantics do not determine whether an engine uses hashing, sorting, or an index.

nodes.label: MapReduce / Mergeable Summaries
nodes.description: MapReduce groups intermediate values by key. Mergeable summaries reduce communication while retaining the information needed for a final result.
explanation: For a mean, retain (sum, count), combine pairs componentwise, and divide once at the end. An unweighted average of worker means fails when partition sizes differ.

A combiner must preserve results when applied to different groupings, including when it is skipped. Associativity and commutativity are useful requirements for unordered aggregation; floating-point rounding still depends on evaluation order.
nodes.boundary: Aggregation algebra does not by itself guarantee exactly-once side effects, deterministic floating-point results, or balanced partitions.

nodes.label: Mergeable Variance / Welford Summaries
nodes.description: A variance summary retains count n, mean mu, and centered squared-deviation sum M2. These statistics can be merged without retaining every observation.
explanation: For nonempty summaries A and B, let n = nA + nB and delta = muB - muA. Merge with mu = muA + delta*nB/n and M2 = M2A + M2B + delta^2*nA*nB/n. An empty summary is the identity and needs a separate branch before division.

Population variance is M2/n for n > 0. Averaging shard variances misses variation between shard means. Each summary merge uses constant arithmetic work and state; a stream can update the same statistics one observation at a time.
nodes.boundary: Population variance and sample variance use different denominators. Empty input needs an explicit convention. Floating-point overflow and rounding remain possible, and different merge orders can produce slightly different results.

nodes.label: External Consistency
nodes.description: External consistency orders transactions serially while preserving real-time precedence: a transaction completed before another begins must precede it in the serial order.
explanation: Serializability requires equivalence to a serial transaction order. External consistency adds the order that clients can observe between non-overlapping transactions.

If T1 commits before T2 begins, a consistent snapshot cannot include T2's effects while omitting T1's. Strong reads started after both commits must reflect both; an explicitly historical snapshot can precede them.
nodes.boundary: Two independent reads are not automatically one snapshot. Clock timestamps alone do not establish a transaction consistency guarantee.

nodes.label: SLI / SLO / Error Budget
nodes.description: An SLI measures a service property. An SLO sets its target. An error budget quantifies the failures allowed under a specified target and measurement window.
explanation: For N > 0 eligible requests, B bad requests, and success target S, observed success is 1 − B/N and the allowed bad-event count is N(1 − S). Budget consumption is B/[N(1 − S)] when the denominator is positive.
Define eligible events, observation window, and measurement location before calculating the ratio. A request-based budget and a time-based availability budget have different denominators.
nodes.boundary: A request error fraction cannot be converted directly into outage duration. An SLO target alone is not an SLA with contractual consequences.

nodes.label: Token Bucket / Rate Limiting
nodes.description: A token bucket limits sustained admission while allowing bounded bursts. Requests consume credit that refills at a fixed rate up to a capacity.
explanation: For capacity C, rate r, elapsed time Δt, and previous credit b, refill to min(C, b + rΔt). Admit a unit-cost request only when this balance is at least one, then subtract one.
Retain fractional credit and update the timestamp on each refill. Shared buckets need atomic refill-and-consume decisions; independent replica buckets do not enforce one global quota.
nodes.boundary: Rate, concurrent in-flight work, and queue size are different limits. A token bucket is not a guarantee of uniform spacing between requests.

nodes.label: Circuit Breaker
nodes.description: A circuit breaker temporarily rejects calls to an unhealthy dependency, then permits bounded probes to test recovery.
explanation: Closed allows calls and records outcomes. Open rejects locally until the recovery policy permits a transition. Half-open allows limited trial calls before restoring normal traffic or reopening.

Choose explicit failure thresholds, observation windows, timeout behavior, and recovery criteria. Concurrent callers must coordinate probe admission to avoid releasing a new burst into a failing service.
nodes.boundary: A circuit breaker does not make retries safe, replace a timeout, or enforce a request-rate quota. Local rejections are not downstream failures.

nodes.label: Optimistic Concurrency / Conditional Writes
nodes.description: Optimistic concurrency detects conflicts when a write commits. A conditional write changes state only if a version or state predicate still holds atomically.
explanation: A version check such as If-Match rejects a stale replacement. After a conflict, reread the current state and recompute the intended change before retrying.
A state predicate can enforce a local invariant directly, such as stock >= requested quantity before subtracting stock in the same atomic operation.
nodes.boundary: A separate read and write do not provide an atomic condition. Conditional mutation alone does not deduplicate repeated business requests or establish a multi-item transaction.

nodes.label: Idempotency / Safe Retries
nodes.description: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated as when applied once. A request identifier can extend this property to operations with business side effects.
explanation: A lost response leaves the caller uncertain whether an operation committed. Retrying a decrement can apply the change twice even if every individual decrement is atomic.

Bind an idempotency key to the request intent. Coordinate recording that key, applying the mutation, and retaining its result so duplicate submissions return the earlier outcome. Define key scope, retention, and behavior for the same key with different parameters.
nodes.boundary: A timeout does not prove failure. A stock predicate, transport retry, FIFO delivery, or expiring cache entry alone does not guarantee one business effect.

nodes.label: Message Ordering / FIFO Groups
nodes.description: A message group defines an ordering boundary. Independent groups can make progress concurrently without a total order across all messages.
explanation: If A1 precedes A2 and B1 precedes B2, six complete interleavings respect these two constraints: choose the two A positions from four slots.
Choose grouping keys that match the business invariant, then process effects in group order. Delivery, handler completion, visibility timeouts, and duplicate effects require separate reasoning.
nodes.boundary: FIFO delivery does not serialize arbitrary asynchronous side effects. A mathematical set of valid schedules does not promise that a queue implements every schedule.

nodes.label: Consistent Hashing
nodes.description: Consistent hashing maps keys and routing tokens into one stable hash space so membership changes move a limited ownership range.
explanation: In a clockwise ring, a key belongs to the first token at or after its hash, with wraparound. A sorted token array supports this lookup with binary search.

Inserting a token transfers the interval from the previous token, exclusive, to the new token, inclusive. Virtual tokens can improve balance; replication must select distinct physical owners when required.
nodes.boundary: Limited remapping does not imply equal load, automatic data migration, or consistency during reconfiguration. One hot key can remain a bottleneck.

nodes.label: GPU Coalescing / Scan / Reduction
nodes.description: GPU algorithms must coordinate memory access, participating threads, and dependency depth as well as total arithmetic work.
explanation: Coalescing groups neighboring lane accesses into memory transactions. Under the stated 32-byte segment model, 32 aligned four-byte contiguous loads touch four segments; a one-word shift touches five.

A work-efficient exclusive scan has O(n) work and O(log n) dependency depth. A reduction combines inputs into a total. Participation masks and synchronization are part of correctness; floating-point results can change with the reduction tree.
nodes.boundary: Operation count and dependency depth do not predict GPU wall time. Transaction rules depend on architecture, and warp masks do not supply values for absent lanes.

nodes.label: Distributed Cache Coherence / Leases
nodes.description: Distributed cache coherence concerns how cached values track authoritative updates. A fill lease can reject an old in-flight read after invalidation.
explanation: In cache-aside, a reader can miss, read an old database value, pause, and refill after a writer commits and deletes the cache entry. Deleting after the database write does not eliminate that interleaving.
Grant a per-key fill token and invalidate it on deletion. Check the token atomically when accepting a fill. A delayed reader with an invalid token cannot repopulate that entry with its old value.
nodes.boundary: This lease protects the illustrated stale-fill race. It is not a CPU cache-coherence protocol, a normal TTL, or a proof of globally serializable database and cache reads.

nodes.label: Floyd–Warshall / All-pairs Shortest Paths
nodes.description: Floyd–Warshall computes shortest-path costs between every pair of vertices by expanding the set of permitted intermediate vertices.
explanation: Initialize d[i][i] = 0, direct edges to their minimum weight, and missing edges to infinity. For each intermediate vertex k, update d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) for every i and j.

Keep k as the outer loop so each stage has a complete intermediate-vertex meaning. The algorithm uses O(V³) time and O(V²) storage for V vertices. A small alphabet of directed character conversions is a natural application.
nodes.boundary: Unreachable pairs remain infinite and must not be treated as free conversions. Negative cycles can make finite shortest-path costs undefined for affected pairs.

nodes.label: Graph Core / Degree Peeling
nodes.description: For an undirected graph, the k-core is the greatest induced subgraph whose vertices all have degree at least k within that subgraph. Repeatedly removing vertices of degree below k finds it.
explanation: Initialize degrees and enqueue every vertex below the threshold. Removing a vertex reduces each surviving neighbor's degree; enqueue a neighbor when it becomes ineligible. Queue processing with adjacency lists takes O(V + E) time and O(V + E) total storage.

Any feasible induced subgraph with minimum degree at least k survives every removal: a vertex currently below k cannot belong to such a subgraph. This invariant proves both the pruning rule and the maximality of the remainder. A required vertex removed during peeling makes a constrained planting problem impossible.
nodes.boundary: Use current degrees after removals. Core membership differs from connected-component membership; even a 2-core can contain a bridge joining two cyclic regions.

nodes.label: Squared-distance Sums / Coordinate Moments
nodes.description: Expanding squared Euclidean distance separates fixed point-set statistics from the query, turning a scan over all stored points into a constant-size calculation in fixed dimension.
explanation: For n points (x_i, y_i), retain Sx = Σx_i, Sy = Σy_i, and Q = Σ(x_i² + y_i²). At query (a, b), the total squared distance is n(a² + b²) − 2aSx − 2bSy + Q.

Build these moments in O(n) time and evaluate q two-dimensional queries in O(q) time, using O(1) aggregate state. With modular output, reduce the expanded expression consistently and use arithmetic wide enough for every product.
nodes.boundary: The expansion is for squared distances. It does not give the sum of ordinary Euclidean distances. Coordinates and aggregate products can exceed safe integer ranges even when each coordinate fits individually.
